# Understanding `_set` in Django

The `_set` attribute in Django is an automatically created reverse relation accessor that allows you to access related objects from the "many" side of a one-to-many relationship.

## How Django Creates Relationships

When you define a foreign key relationship in Django:

```python
class PropertyType(models.Model):
    key = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    # other fields...

class ContractProperty(models.Model):
    property_type = models.ForeignKey(PropertyType, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    # other fields...
```

Django automatically creates:

1. A `property_type` field on `ContractProperty` (the one you defined)
2. A `contractproperty_set` attribute on `PropertyType` (automatically created)

## Why the `_set` Naming Convention?

The `_set` naming follows this pattern:
- It uses the lowercase name of the model containing the ForeignKey
- It appends `_set` to indicate it's a collection (set) of objects

## How to Use `_set`

```python
# Get a PropertyType
property_type = PropertyType.objects.get(id=1)

# Get all ContractProperty objects related to this PropertyType
related_properties = property_type.contractproperty_set.all()
```

## Customizing the Reverse Relationship Name

If you don't like the default `_set` name, you can customize it:

```python
class ContractProperty(models.Model):
    property_type = models.ForeignKey(
        PropertyType, 
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='properties'  # This changes the name from contractproperty_set
    )
```

Now you would use:
```python
property_type.properties.all()  # Instead of property_type.contractproperty_set.all()
```

## In Your Example Code

In your original code:
```python
contract.wip_version.contractproperty_set.select_related("property_type").all()
```

This is traversing:
1. From a `contract` object
2. To its `wip_version` (another related object)
3. To all `ContractProperty` objects related to that version through the auto-generated `contractproperty_set` accessor

This pattern indicates that your `Contract` model likely has a relationship to some "Version" model, which in turn has a one-to-many relationship with `ContractProperty`.
